Logical Operators

CautionPrerequisites
  • None
TipDefinition 0.1 - Statement

A “statement” is a sentence which can be classified as either true or false, which we will abbreviate with T and F.

TipNotation 0.1 - Logical operators

Let \(p, q\) each be statements.

  1. \(\neg p\) – not \(p\), “negation” of \(p\)
  2. \(p\land q\) – \(p\) “and” \(q\)
  3. \(p\lor q\) – \(p\) “or” \(q\)
  4. \(p\implies q\) – \(p\) “implies” \(q\)
  5. \(p\iff q\) – \(p\) “if and only if” \(q\), meaning \(p\implies q\) and \(p\impliedby q\)
TipDefinition 0.2 - Truth Table

A “truth table” is a table that lists whether a statements with a logical operator yields T or F.

WarningExample 0.1

The above definition of truth table is left vague on purpose, since it’s easier to show an example rather than describing it. Let \(p,q\) be statements. Consider the following table;

\(p\) \(q\) \(\neg p\) \(\neg q\) \(p\land q\) \(p\lor q\) \(p\implies q\) \(p\iff q\)
T T
T F
F T
F F

where the first two columns are given. What will the next statements yield for each combination of \(p\) and \(q\)?

ImportantAnswer

For \(\neg p\), we yield the opposite of \(p\), meaning if \(p\) is T then \(\neg p\) is F and vice versa. The analog is true for \(\neg q\).

\(p\land q\) is T only when both of \(p\) and \(q\) are T, otherwise it is F. > \(p\lor q\) is F only when both of \(p\) and \(q\) are F, otherwise it is T.

\(p\implies q\) is trickier. First the statement itself is saying “if \(p\) is T, then \(q\) is T”. So if both are T, then this statement is also T. If \(p\) is T and \(q\) is F, this statement is not satisfied, thus it is F. If \(p\) is F and \(q\) is T, we still yield T, since there is no information saying otherwise. If both are F, then similarly, we yield T, since this is still possible.

\(p\iff q\) requires that the symbol for both sides must match each other.

\(p\) \(q\) \(\neg p\) \(\neg q\) \(p\land q\) \(p\lor q\) \(p\implies q\) \(p\iff q\)
T T F F T T T T
T F F T F T F F
F T T F F T T F
F F T T F F T T
TipDefinition 0.3 - Tautology and Contradiction

If a statement is always true, then that statement is a “tautology”.

If a statement is always false, then that statement is a “contradiction”.

TipDefinition 0.4 - Converse, Inverse, Contrapositive
  1. The “converse” of \(p\implies q\) is \(q\implies p\)
  2. The “inverse” of \(p\implies q\) is \((\neg p)\implies (\neg q)\)
  3. The “contrapositive” of \(p\implies q\) is \((\neg q)\implies (\neg p)\)

These phrases are used in various proof techniques.

WarningExample 0.2 - Truth Table Extended

Extend the truth table above to include the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of \(p\implies q\).

ImportantAnswer
\(p\) \(q\) \(p\implies q\) \(p\iff q\) \(q\implies p\) \((\neg p)\implies (\neg q)\) \((\neg q)\implies (\neg p)\)
T T T T T T T
T F F F T T F
F T T F F F T
F F T T T T T

Notably, the contrapositive is logically equivalent to \(p\implies q\).
